opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the more underappreciated parts of the AI story. There are a few distinct channels through which scale feeds back on itself, and they compound.

The most obvious is on the training side. Training a frontier model is a huge fixed cost, but once you've trained it, the marginal cost of serving another user or running another copy is comparatively small. That's a classic increasing-returns structure: the more widely you deploy, the more you amortize that fixed investment, and the more you can afford to spend on the next, larger training run. So revenue from deployment funds bigger models, bigger models are more capable and attract more use, and the loop continues.

A second channel is learning by doing, on the hardware and the algorithms. As the industry produces more chips, builds more data centers, and runs more experiments, costs fall. We've seen pretty steady improvements in algorithmic efficiency, where the compute needed to reach a given level of performance falls substantially year over year. A lot of that comes from having more researchers, more compute for experimentation, and more deployment feedback. Scale makes the inputs cheaper, which makes further scale cheaper.

The third channel is the one I find most interesting from an economic-growth perspective. In standard growth models, ideas are non-rival: once discovered, they can be used everywhere at once. The constraint historically has been that the number of people generating ideas grows slowly, roughly with population. If AI systems can substitute for human labor, including research labor, then you can effectively increase the "population" of researchers by building more compute. Now you have a loop where output gets reinvested into compute, which produces more AI workers, which produce more output and more ideas. That's the mechanism that, in a lot of semi-endogenous growth models, gives you accelerating rather than steady growth.

There are real frictions, of course. You can hit bottlenecks in energy, chip fabrication capacity, data, or tasks that remain hard to automate, and Baumol-type effects mean the slowest-to-automate parts of the economy can end up dominating costs. So I wouldn't say increasing returns guarantee explosive growth. But when you look at the structure of the technology, with high fixed costs, low marginal costs, rapid learning curves, and the potential to automate idea production itself, it seems quite plausible that we get a regime where returns to scale are substantially stronger than anything we've seen in the industrial era. I think that's something policymakers and economists should take seriously, rather than assuming AI is just another general-purpose technology that adds a bit to productivity growth.

r001.rationale: The response says training has a huge fixed cost and deployment spreads that investment across more users, making the investment more economical.

r002.rationale: It does not explain that higher API request volume enables batching or improves hardware utilization.

r003.rationale: It discusses lower costs from learning and scale, but does not say those savings are passed to users or make improvements appear faster to them.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So I think there are actually several distinct mechanisms here that often get lumped together, and it's worth separating them.

The first is the classic one: fixed costs. Training a frontier model is an enormous upfront expenditure, hundreds of millions, soon billions of dollars, and then the marginal cost of serving an additional query is quite small by comparison. That's textbook increasing returns to scale. The more users you have, the lower your average cost per unit of output, which is why you'd expect this to push toward a fairly concentrated market structure, at least at the frontier.

The second mechanism is more interesting from a macroeconomic perspective, and it's about the production of ideas. Traditional growth models, going back to Romer, point out that ideas are non-rival. Once you've figured out how to do something, that knowledge can be used by an arbitrary number of people without being used up. What AI does is make the ideas-producing input itself, the researcher, the engineer, something you can scale by adding compute rather than by waiting for population growth and education. If you can double the number of effective researchers by doubling compute, and the output of those researchers is non-rival, you get a kind of compounding that we haven't really seen before. The scale of the economy feeds back into how much compute you can afford, which feeds back into how fast you improve the technology, and so on.

A third thing I'd point to is that AI systems seem to exhibit returns to scale in the narrow technical sense too. We've seen fairly consistent scaling laws where more compute, more data, and more parameters give you predictable improvements in capability. And crucially, deployment at scale generates data and revenue that funds the next round of scaling. So there's a flywheel where usage, capability, and investment reinforce each other.

Now, I'd caveat all of this. Increasing returns don't mean there are no bottlenecks. Energy, chip fabrication, the physical rollout of robotics if we're talking about the physical economy, regulatory friction, those are all things that can slow the loop down considerably. And historically, people have been too quick to assume that a technology with strong increasing returns will take over everything overnight. But I do think the combination of these mechanisms makes AI quite different from previous general-purpose technologies, and the models in which you get sustained acceleration rather than a one-time level shift are, I'd say, more plausible than most economists currently give them credit for.

r001.rationale: The response says model training has large fixed costs and that more users lower average cost per unit of output, making the fixed investment more economical.

r002.rationale: It does not mention API request volume enabling batching or improving hardware utilization.

r003.rationale: It describes usage, revenue, and investment reinforcing one another, but does not say serving cost savings are passed on to users or make improvements appear faster to them.

astra-6.text:
I think there are a few ways this could happen. One is that developing an AI system involves a large fixed cost, while deploying it to serve an additional user is comparatively cheap. So, as you spread that development cost across more users, the average cost falls. That can make it worthwhile to invest even more in developing the next system, which potentially creates a feedback loop between scale and capability.

Another is that a more capable system can be useful across a wider range of tasks. You're spreading the cost of training across many different applications, rather than having to build a separate system for each one. There are still costs associated with inference and adapting systems to particular uses, but that breadth could be a substantial source of increasing returns.

And then there's the possibility of AI contributing to AI research itself. If greater deployment generates revenue that funds more compute and research, and the resulting systems help make that research more productive, you get another feedback loop.

I wouldn't assume these effects continue without limits. You can encounter bottlenecks in energy, chips, or the ability of organizations to actually use these systems effectively. But they do suggest that the economics could favor very large investments, and potentially a fairly concentrated set of developers.

r001.rationale: The response says spreading the large development cost across more users lowers average cost and makes further investment worthwhile.

r002.rationale: It does not mention API request volume, batching, or improved hardware utilization.

r003.rationale: It does not say serving cost savings are passed on to users or that this makes improvements reach them faster.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are a few mechanisms here. One is that developing an AI system involves a large fixed cost, but then using that system to perform an additional task can be relatively cheap. So if you can spread the cost of training across a much larger number of users and applications, the economics become more favorable.

And as systems become more capable, the range of applications expands. That creates a larger market over which you can amortize those costs, which can justify spending more on developing the next system. So you get a feedback loop: greater investment produces a more capable system, that system serves a larger market, and the larger market supports greater investment.

Another possibility is that AI makes some of the inputs to AI development cheaper—for example, by automating parts of software engineering or research. Then investment in AI could improve your ability to produce further improvements in AI.

But I would distinguish those mechanisms from the claim that returns necessarily keep increasing indefinitely. You can still have diminishing returns to training compute, constraints on deployment, and competition that pushes prices down. The interesting question is whether the expansion in what these systems can economically do outweighs those forces.

r001.rationale: It says training costs can be spread across a much larger number of users and applications, making the economics more favorable.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss higher API request volume enabling batching or improving hardware utilization.

r003.rationale: It does not say that serving-scale cost savings are passed on to users or make improvements appear faster.
